opus-5.5.text:
Language is a wonderful thing, but it's fundamentally a one-dimensional, sequential signal. It's something humans invented to communicate and to compress our thoughts. And because it's generated by us, there's a lot of structure baked into it already. When you train a large model on enormous amounts of text, you're learning from a signal that is, in a sense, already pre-digested by human minds.

The physical world is different. It's three-dimensional, it obeys physics, it unfolds in time, and it exists whether or not anyone describes it. When you look at a scene, your eyes get a 2D projection of a 3D world, and your brain has to recover that structure: where things are, how far away, what's behind what, what happens if I reach out and push this cup. That inverse problem is ill-posed and much harder in many ways than predicting the next token.

If you go back in evolutionary history, perception and the ability to act in a 3D environment came hundreds of millions of years before language. Animals developed vision and navigation and manipulation long before anyone said a word. So in a way, spatial intelligence is more foundational. It's the scaffolding that much of our intelligence, including language, sits on top of.

So when I talk about spatial intelligence, I mean the ability of a machine to perceive, reason about, generate, and interact with the 3D world, not just describe it in words. A language model can tell you a lot about a room if you've written about rooms. But to really understand the geometry, to imagine walking through it, to plan how a robot would move in it, or to let a creator build a new world, you need models whose native representation is space and time. I think language models and spatial models will be deeply complementary, but you can't get to the full picture of intelligence through language alone.

r001.rationale: The response calls language and spatial models deeply complementary, but does not say they share architectural components.

r002.rationale: It contrasts language as a one-dimensional sequential signal with a physical world that is three-dimensional and unfolds in time.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think this is really the question I've been living with for the past several years.

Language is an extraordinary achievement, but it's also a very particular kind of signal. It's one-dimensional, it's sequential, it's discrete, and most importantly, it's a purely generative artifact of the human mind. There's no language out there in nature. Every token a language model learns from was produced by a person who already understood the world and compressed that understanding into words. So in a sense, large language models are learning from a lossy, highly abstracted summary of human experience.

Spatial intelligence is something much older. Evolutionarily, it predates language by hundreds of millions of years. The first trilobites that developed primitive eyes some five hundred and forty million years ago weren't describing anything. They were perceiving, navigating, hunting, avoiding predators. Intelligence, for most of its history on this planet, has been about understanding a three-dimensional world, reasoning about it, and acting in it. Language came very, very late, as a layer on top of that.

So when I think about spatial intelligence, I'm thinking about the ability to perceive the 3D structure of a scene, to reason about what's where and how objects relate to each other, to predict what will happen if I move or if something else moves, and then to act, to plan and intervene in the world. That loop of perception, reasoning, and action is fundamentally different from predicting the next word.

There's also a data problem that makes it harder. The internet gave us trillions of tokens of text almost for free. We don't have anything like that for the physical world. Video helps, but video is a 2D projection, and most of it was never captured with the goal of teaching a machine about geometry, physics, or affordances. So a lot of what we're doing at World Labs and in the broader field is really about generating worlds, building models that can produce consistent, navigable 3D environments, and using that as both a capability and a training signal.

I want to be clear that I don't see this as spatial versus language. Humans have both, and they reinforce each other. But if we want AI that can help a surgeon, a firefighter, an elderly person living alone, or a designer building something that doesn't exist yet, we need machines that genuinely understand space. Language alone won't get us there.

r001.rationale: The response says spatial and language intelligence can reinforce each other, but it does not suggest their generative models will share architectural components.

r002.rationale: It contrasts language as a one-dimensional, sequential signal with spatial intelligence’s focus on perceiving and reasoning about a three-dimensional world and acting within it.

astra-6.text:
I think of spatial intelligence as the ability to understand and interact with the three-dimensional world. When you look at a room, you don’t just identify a chair and a table. You understand their relationships, where you can move, what you can reach, and what might happen if you push something. A lot of that understanding never needs to be put into words.

Language is an incredibly powerful way to represent and communicate knowledge. But a description of the world is different from the world itself. Imagine picking up a cup of coffee: you need to understand its geometry, estimate how to grasp it, and adjust your movement as you make contact. Describing that action and successfully performing it are different capabilities.

So I see spatial intelligence as complementary to language. The challenge is to build systems that connect perception, prediction, and action—that can reason about how the physical world works and what their actions will change.

r001.rationale: The response calls spatial intelligence complementary to language and discusses connecting perception, prediction, and action, but it does not suggest that spatial and language generative models will share architectural components.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the physical three-dimensional world with descriptions in language, but does not identify the structural difference as a 3D/4D spatial world versus a one-dimensional generative signal.

sol-6.1.text:
I see spatial intelligence as the ability to understand and interact with the three-dimensional world. It’s understanding where things are, how they relate to one another, how they move, and what might happen when you take an action.

Language gives us a powerful way to describe that world, but describing something is different from acting in it. You can describe a glass of water beautifully, but picking it up requires understanding its shape, its position, how to grasp it, and how to move it without spilling. Much of that knowledge is never explicitly put into words.

So I see these capabilities as complementary. Language helps us communicate and reason about the world; spatial intelligence connects perception, prediction, and action within it.

r001.rationale: The response calls spatial intelligence and language complementary, but does not say their generative models will share architectural components.

r002.rationale: It describes spatial intelligence as involving a three-dimensional world and contrasts description with action, but does not identify a fundamental structural difference between a 3D/4D world and a one-dimensional generative signal.
